newsitem.title: USA: Kodak sues ex-employees for stealing technology.
newsitem.headline: Kodak sues ex-employees for stealing technology.

text.p: Eastman Kodak Co. said Friday it was suing two former employees, a research centre supervisor and a developmental engineer, for allegedly stealing and selling "tens of millions" of dollars worth of its photography technology to competitors.

The suit, filed in federal court in Rochester, names Harold Worden, a former supervisor at Kodak Park, the firm's main film manufacturing and research and development centre, and Kurt Strobl, an engineer who left the company on Wednesday, Kodak spokesman James Blamphin said.
Kodak believes the value of the information stolen and sold to potential competitors "around the world" runs into the "tens of millions" of dollars, Blamphin said.

The suit was filed after a year-long probe by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the U.S. Attorney's office, Blamphin said. He said the probe, which continues, was begun at the request of the company.
In a letter to employees released Friday, Kodak said Worden set up a consulting firm, Worden Enterprises Inc., after he retired from the company in 1992.

Between 1993 and 1995, the letter said, Worden Enterprises provided technical and engineering services to various clients, including companies that manufacture products that compete with those sold by Kodak.
Worden sought to market the services of about 60 "associates" as well as himself by emphasising their careers as Kodak employees, it said.
The "associates" had significant technical knowledge in a variety of areas related to the manufacture of photographic films, acetate and photographic paper, it said.
In a search of Worden's home and office, the FBI seized about 40,000 original Kodak documents or copies that appeared to be taken from the company, according to the letter.
Kodak has about 19,000 employees at Kodak Park in Rochester and spends about $1 billion a year on research, Blamphin said.
Blamphin said Worden was a technical associate in a supervisory position and Strobl was a senior engineer.
Worden worked on the "401 machine," a four-story-high machine that makes clear plastic sheets that are coated with liquid emulsions to make film, he said.

In another letter dated Oct. 31 to Kodak employees and retirees, also released Friday, the company asked for help in identifying the possible compromising of Kodak confidential information by their current or former colleagues or contractors.
Kodak's stock fell $1.50 to $80.375 on the New York Stock Exchange in late morning trading.
